title: My AI Checklist
subject: AI-Literacy
description: Practice on protecting your personal information from apps and AI, and on honestly and responsibly disclosing how AI helped with schoolwork or creative work, drawn from the 'My AI Checklist' worksheet and the true story of artist Boris Eldagsen.

questions.question: In the 'My AI Checklist' worksheet, Question 1 asks you to look at some apps and tick every type of information each one might ______.
questions.explanation: Question 1 instructs: 'For each one, tick every type of information it might collect.'

questions.question: Which of these apps are listed in the apps-and-information checklist table? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The table lists exactly YouTube, a mobile game, an AI study helper, and a photo filter app.

questions.question: Which of these types of personal information are listed as columns in the checklist table? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The table has exactly five columns: name, location, what you watch/play, voice, and face/photo.

questions.question: How many different apps are shown in the 'My AI Checklist' information table?
questions.explanation: The table lists four apps: YouTube, a mobile game, an AI study helper, and a photo filter app.

questions.question: How many types of personal information are listed as columns in the checklist table?
questions.explanation: There are five columns: name, location, what you watch/play, voice, and face/photo.

questions.question: Which type of information would a Photo Filter app most likely need to work?
questions.explanation: Photo filter apps edit pictures, so they need access to your face/photo to apply the effect.

questions.question: An AI study helper that answers questions you speak out loud would most likely need to collect...
questions.explanation: To understand spoken questions, a voice-based helper needs to record and process your voice.

questions.question: YouTube recommending videos based on what you have already seen is mainly using...
questions.explanation: Video recommendations are built from your viewing history, matching the 'What you watch/Play' column.

questions.question: A mobile game that tracks your scores and playing habits mainly collects...
questions.explanation: Tracking scores and habits is exactly the kind of 'Play' activity the checklist column describes.

questions.question: Which of these would a Photo Filter app almost certainly NOT need to collect just to apply a filter to your picture?
options: Your permission to use the camera
questions.explanation: A bank password has nothing to do with editing photos; it is an unrelated, unnecessary piece of information, even though it may look like a normal thing an app could ask for.

questions.question: True or False: According to the checklist, every single app in the table must collect all five types of information listed.
questions.explanation: The worksheet asks you to tick only the info each app 'might' collect — different apps collect different things, not all five for every app.

questions.question: True or False: The checklist in Question 1 is meant to help you think about what personal information different apps might gather.
questions.explanation: That is exactly the purpose stated in Question 1's instructions.

questions.question: Select all the pieces of information a food delivery app is said to learn about you, according to Question 2.
options: Which family member's account you are using
questions.explanation: Question 2 states the app learns 'your name, your address, what you eat, when you usually order, and which family member's account you are using.'

questions.question: According to Question 2, what does the food delivery app in the example use AI for?
options: To suggest what you should order
To play music while you eat
questions.explanation: The text states the app 'uses AI to suggest what you should order.'

questions.question: Which country is mentioned in the food delivery app example in Question 2?
questions.explanation: The worksheet says: 'A food delivery app in India uses AI...'

questions.question: The food delivery app example learns 'which family member's account you are using.' Why might this be a privacy concern?
options: It means the app can link information to more than just you, including other family members
It means the app will delete the account
It means the food will be delivered late
It means the app cannot suggest any food at all
questions.explanation: Knowing whose account is used means the app can connect ordering habits to specific people, extending privacy concerns beyond just the one user placing the order.

questions.question: Question 2a asks you to circle the pieces of information you would be comfortable sharing. Which options are given to choose from? (Select all)
questions.explanation: Question 2a lists exactly: Name, Address, Eating habits, Order time, Family member's account.

questions.question: What is the difference the worksheet asks you to think about in Question 2b?
options: The difference between what you WOULD share and what you SHOULD share
The difference between apps and websites
The difference between AI and humans
The difference between fast and slow internet
questions.explanation: Question 2b literally asks: 'Is there a difference between what you WOULD share and what you SHOULD share?'

questions.question: True or False: Something you feel comfortable sharing is always something that is safe to share.
questions.explanation: Question 2b specifically points out there can be a difference between what you WOULD share (comfort) and what you SHOULD share (safety/appropriateness) — they are not always the same.

questions.question: According to Question 2c, what does the app do if it never asks permission before collecting your data?
questions.explanation: The text says directly: 'The app never asks permission — it just collects.'

questions.question: Question 2c raises the question of who is responsible for protecting your information when an app collects data without asking permission. What is this question inviting you to reflect on?
options: Who should be responsible for protecting your personal information
Which app has the best design
questions.explanation: Question 2c is explicitly a reflection prompt about who should be responsible for protecting a user's personal information.

questions.question: Select all statements about the apps-and-information checklist (Question 1) that are TRUE.
options: It lists more than one type of app
It lists more than one type of personal information
It asks you to tick every type of info an app might collect
It gives you the definite correct answer for each app so there is nothing to think about
questions.explanation: The worksheet is a reflection/reasoning exercise — it does not hand you a definite official answer for each app, so 'nothing to think about' is false.

questions.question: Which worksheet task comes first in the 'My AI Checklist' activity — the apps information table or the food delivery app example?
questions.explanation: Question 1 (the apps table) precedes Question 2 (the food delivery example) in the worksheet's order.

questions.question: Why does the worksheet follow the apps checklist with a detailed food delivery app example?
options: To show concretely how an app can gather several kinds of personal information at once
To teach you how to cook
To advertise a specific delivery company
questions.explanation: The detailed food delivery scenario illustrates, with a concrete case, how one app can combine name/address/habits/timing/account data — building on the general checklist idea.

questions.question: True or False: The worksheet names a specific food delivery company.
questions.explanation: The text only says 'A food delivery app in India' — it does not name any specific brand.

questions.question: What overall skill are Question 1 and Question 2 together mainly building?
options: Noticing what personal information apps and AI tools might collect
Learning to record a voice note
questions.explanation: Both tasks are about spotting what information gets collected, laying groundwork for the chapter's privacy theme.

questions.question: In Question 3, which statement reflects the most responsible way to use AI for schoolwork?
options: If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.
If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.
It doesn't matter if no one finds out.
AI should never be used for any homework.
questions.explanation: Being honest about how much AI helped matches the chapter's whole message (as also shown later by the Boris Eldagsen story); the other statements are misconceptions given in the same question.

questions.question: Select all the statements from Question 3 that are misconceptions (not the most responsible view).
options: If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.
If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.
It doesn't matter if no one finds out.
questions.explanation: Statement 2 ('If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped') reflects honesty; statements 1 and 3 are misconceptions — small edits don't make AI work 'fully yours', and honesty matters even if undetected.

questions.question: True or False: Changing a few words in an AI-written essay is enough to make the whole essay truly your own work.
questions.explanation: The ideas, structure, and most of the wording still came from AI — a few word swaps do not change who really created the content.

questions.question: True or False: According to the values in this chapter, it is fine to hide your use of AI as long as nobody ever finds out.
questions.explanation: The chapter's message (also shown by the Boris Eldagsen story) is that honesty matters regardless of whether you get caught — this is exactly the misconception the worksheet warns against.

questions.question: Which value is Question 3 in the worksheet mainly testing?
options: Honesty about how much AI helped with your work
questions.explanation: The three statements are all about how honest a student is about AI's role in their work.

questions.question: If a student uses AI to write most of an essay but tells the teacher AI helped, which statement from Question 3 are they following?
options: 'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.'
'If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.'
'It doesn't matter if no one finds out.'
questions.explanation: This matches statement 2 exactly: 'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.'

questions.question: How many statements are given to choose from in Question 3?
questions.explanation: Question 3 gives exactly three statements to tick from.

questions.question: A student edits only three words of an AI-written paragraph and submits it as fully their own. Which statement's mistaken idea are they acting on?
options: 'If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.'
'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.'
'It doesn't matter if no one finds out.'
questions.explanation: This matches the misconception: 'If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.'

questions.question: True or False: Question 3 asks you to tick the statement you agree with LEAST.
questions.explanation: It actually asks you to 'tick the statement you agree with most.'

questions.question: What does Question 3 ask you to do?
options: Tick the statement you agree with most
Draw a picture of an app
questions.explanation: The instruction reads: 'Tick the statement you agree with most.'

questions.question: Which of these ideas connect Question 3 to the Boris Eldagsen story later in the worksheet? (Select all)
options: Both are about being honest about how AI was used
Both talk about telling the truth even when you don't have to
Both are only about grammar mistakes
questions.explanation: Both Question 3 and the Eldagsen story are fundamentally about honestly disclosing AI's role in your work, and about telling the truth even when it isn't required.

questions.question: Why is 'it doesn't matter if no one finds out' considered a misconception in this chapter?
options: Because honesty about AI use matters on its own, not just to avoid being caught
Because AI always gets found out eventually
Because teachers can always tell AI-written work
Because it is technically true and not a misconception
questions.explanation: The chapter's values (echoed by Eldagsen's story) treat honesty as important in itself, independent of whether someone happens to notice.

questions.question: True or False: Question 3 is about choosing between statements related to using AI to help write an essay.
questions.explanation: All three statements in Question 3 are about AI helping write an essay.

questions.question: Which of these best explains why simply changing a few words doesn't make AI-written work 'fully yours'?
options: The main ideas, structure, and most of the content still came from the AI
Because the teacher will always know
Because AI writing is always wrong
Because words can never be changed
questions.explanation: The main ideas, structure, and most of the content still came from the AI, even if a few words are changed.

questions.question: A student says: 'AI helped me a lot, but I only changed some words, so it's basically all mine, and there's no need to mention AI since no one would know anyway.' Which two misconceptions from Question 3 is this student combining? (Select all)
options: 'If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.'
'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.'
'It doesn't matter if no one finds out.'
questions.explanation: The statement mixes both misconceptions — claiming minor edits equal full ownership, and treating secrecy as an excuse not to disclose.

questions.question: In Question 3, which statement encourages disclosing (telling others) that AI helped with your work?
options: 'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.'
'If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.'
'It doesn't matter if no one finds out.'
questions.explanation: Statement 2, 'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped', encourages disclosure.

questions.question: True or False: The worksheet presents three statements in Question 3, and only one of them matches the chapter's honesty message.
questions.explanation: Only 'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped' matches the chapter's honesty message; the other two are misconceptions.

questions.question: A student changes only the introduction of an AI-written essay and keeps everything else. Based on the chapter's message, is this essay now 'fully theirs'?
options: No — most of the content and ideas are still the AI's
Yes, because they wrote the introduction
Yes, because they read it before submitting
Yes, because AI cannot write introductions
questions.explanation: Most of the content and ideas are still the AI's, so changing just the introduction does not make the whole essay the student's own work.

questions.question: What kind of school work is used as the example in Question 3?
questions.explanation: Question 3 talks about 'an essay written by AI.'

questions.question: How does Question 3 connect to the overall guiding question of the worksheet, 'Does using AI protect me — and represent me?'
options: It checks whether you represent your own work honestly when AI has helped
It checks whether your essay is grammatically perfect
It checks how fast you can write
It checks whether you like reading
questions.explanation: Question 3 checks whether a student represents their own work honestly when AI has helped, connecting directly to the 'represent me' part of the guiding question.

questions.question: True or False: According to the chapter, saying AI helped with your work makes your work worth less.
questions.explanation: The chapter's message (through both Question 3 and the Eldagsen story) is that being honest about AI's help is the responsible choice, not something that reduces the value of your work.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three statements listed in Question 3?
options: 'AI should always write my homework for me.'
'If I change a few words in an essay written by AI, it becomes fully mine.'
'If AI writes most of it, I should say it helped.'
'It doesn't matter if no one finds out.'
questions.explanation: 'AI should always write my homework for me' is not one of the three statements; the real ones are about changing words, saying AI helped, and not being found out.

questions.question: Question 3 is part of which worksheet difficulty section?
questions.explanation: Question 3 appears at the top of the 'Powering up' section (Level ★★).

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: According to Question 4b, what are the three named 'levels' of AI help listed (besides 'None of these')?
options: The Spark, The Editor, The Researcher
The Beginner, The Expert, The Master
The Helper, The Checker, The Finder
The Starter, The Fixer, The Seeker
questions.explanation: Question 4b lists exactly: The Spark, The Editor, The Researcher, and None of these.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: What does 'The Spark' level mean, according to the worksheet?
questions.explanation: Question 4b defines: 'The Spark (It gave ideas)'.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: What does 'The Editor' level mean, according to the worksheet?
questions.explanation: Question 4b defines: 'The Editor (It improved my work)'.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: What does 'The Researcher' level mean, according to the worksheet?
questions.explanation: Question 4b defines: 'The Researcher (It helped find information)'.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: A writing/spelling app that corrects your grammar mistakes is acting mostly as...
questions.explanation: Correcting spelling/grammar matches 'It improved my work', which is exactly how 'The Editor' is defined.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: A tool that gives you an answer to a factual question is acting mostly as...
questions.explanation: 'Helped find information' matches 'The Researcher'.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: A tool that just gives you a first idea to start your project, without doing the work for you, is acting mostly as...
questions.explanation: 'Gave me ideas' matches 'The Spark'.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: If a digital tool BOTH gave you an idea AND then corrected your grammar, which single level best captures the part where 'it gave me ideas'?
questions.explanation: 'Gave me ideas' is specifically the Spark's definition, even if the same tool also helped in other ways.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Select all of the digital learning tools mentioned as examples in Question 4.
questions.explanation: Exactly these four tools are named in Question 4: Google search, YouTube for homework help, a voice assistant, and a writing/spelling app.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: How many 'how did it help you' options are listed to choose from in Question 4a?
questions.explanation: Question 4a lists exactly five options, plus the 'not used any tool' option makes five total choices.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Select all the options given in Question 4a for 'How did it help you?'
options: It explained something I didn't understand
I have not used any tool like this yet
It wrote my whole essay for me
questions.explanation: Question 4a lists exactly these five choices; 'It wrote my whole essay for me' is not one of them.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: True or False: 'None of these' is one of the choices for Question 4b (choosing a level).
questions.explanation: Question 4b's four choices are The Spark, The Editor, The Researcher, and None of these.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: True or False: The three named levels in Question 4b are The Spark, The Editor, and The Researcher.
questions.explanation: These are exactly the three named levels given in Question 4b.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Which level involves a tool making direct improvements or corrections to work you already wrote, rather than starting something new or looking things up?
questions.explanation: 'The Editor' is defined as 'It improved my work', which fits fixing/improving already-written work.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Select all levels that describe a tool that does NOT simply write the whole assignment for the student.
questions.explanation: All three levels describe forms of assistance (ideas, improvement, information) rather than the AI completing the whole assignment by itself.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: True or False: According to the worksheet, using a voice assistant automatically means you are at 'The Researcher' level.
questions.explanation: The worksheet doesn't assign one fixed level to each named tool — the level depends on HOW the tool helped (ideas vs. improving work vs. finding information), not which tool it was.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Question 4 first asks you to think of a tool you used, then asks about...
options: How it helped you, and which 'level' that help matches
Whether you like the tool's colour scheme
questions.explanation: After naming the tool, Question 4a/4b ask how it helped and which 'level' that help matches.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: In Question 4a, which choice would you tick if you have never used a digital learning tool?
options: I have not used any tool like this yet
questions.explanation: Question 4a's last option is exactly 'I have not used any tool like this yet.'

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: True or False: 'None of these' appears as an option in both Question 4a and Question 4b, worded identically.
questions.explanation: 'I have not used any tool like this yet' is the closest option in 4a, while 'None of these' specifically appears as a choice in 4b — they are worded differently in the two sub-questions.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Question 4c asks whether, if you used AI/a digital tool for schoolwork, you...
questions.explanation: Question 4c asks: 'If you used it, did you tell your teacher or parent?'

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: A student used an AI tool to brainstorm ideas for a story, then wrote the story mostly themselves. Which level best fits, based on the worksheet's definitions?
questions.explanation: 'Gave me ideas' is literally the Spark's definition; the tool did not fix grammar or find facts here, so Editor/Researcher fit less well.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: A student asked an AI tool to explain a maths concept they were stuck on, and it gave them the information they needed. Which level best matches?
questions.explanation: 'Helped find information' matches 'The Researcher'.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Select all statements that are TRUE about the three levels (Spark, Editor, Researcher).
options: Each one describes a different kind of help a digital tool can give
They all mean exactly the same thing
'The Editor' is about improving already-written work
questions.explanation: The three levels are distinct kinds of help, not synonyms of each other.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Which worksheet question introduces the Spark/Editor/Researcher levels?
questions.explanation: The three levels are introduced in Question 4b.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: True or False: The Spark/Editor/Researcher levels are described inside Question 4, which is in the 'Powering up' section.
questions.explanation: Question 4 is in the 'Powering up' (Level ★★) section, along with the level definitions.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'The Editor' level?
options: Making existing work better, e.g. fixing spelling and grammar
questions.explanation: 'The Editor' means the tool made existing work better, such as fixing spelling and grammar.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'The Researcher' level?
options: Helping you find facts or information
Improving grammar in a finished piece
questions.explanation: 'The Researcher' means the tool helped you find facts or information.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Which of these best matches 'It explained something I didn't understand' from Question 4a, in everyday terms?
options: A tool clarifying or explaining a concept for you
A tool turning off your Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: This describes a tool helping you understand a concept — closest in spirit to a tool giving information or clarifying something, even though the worksheet does not force it into one of the three named levels.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: True or False: Question 4a lists 'I have not used any tool like this yet' as one of its choices.
questions.explanation: This is explicitly the fifth listed option in Question 4a.

questions.topic: Levels of AI Help: Spark, Editor, Researcher
questions.question: Which of these tools is explicitly named in Question 4 as an example of a digital tool used 'for learning'?
questions.explanation: Google search is explicitly named as one of the four example tools in Question 4's introduction.

questions.question: Question 4c is directly about...
options: Whether you told a teacher or parent about using AI/a digital tool
questions.explanation: Question 4c asks whether you told your teacher or parent about using AI/a digital tool.

questions.question: Why might it matter whether a student tells a teacher or parent about using AI for schoolwork?
options: Being open about AI use is part of being honest about how the work was made
Teachers always forbid using any digital tools
Parents need to approve every app on the phone
questions.explanation: Being open about AI use is part of being honest about how the work was made, matching the chapter's honesty theme.

questions.question: True or False: According to the worksheet, telling no one about your AI use is always the safest choice.
questions.explanation: The chapter's overall message (through Question 3 and the Eldagsen story) values telling the truth about how AI was used, not staying silent.

questions.question: Which option in Question 4c shows a student who never actively considered telling anyone?
questions.explanation: 'I didn't think about it' is the option describing a lack of consideration, distinct from 'Yes' or 'No'.

questions.question: Select all the choices offered for whether a student disclosed their AI use, in Question 4c.
questions.explanation: Question 4c offers exactly three choices: Yes, No, and I didn't think about it.

questions.question: A student ticks 'No' for Question 4c and then 'Nervous' for Question 4d. What might the worksheet want them to reflect on next?
options: Whether not telling anyone was really the most honest choice
Whether they liked the essay topic
Whether the food delivery app was accurate
questions.explanation: Reflecting on feelings after a 'No' answer nudges the student to reconsider whether staying silent was really the most honest choice, given the chapter's honesty theme.

questions.question: How does Question 4d ask you to describe your feelings about your past disclosure choice?
questions.explanation: Question 4d offers exactly two feeling words: Confident and Nervous.

questions.question: In which section (Level) of the worksheet do Questions 4c and 4d appear?
options: They are not in any section
questions.explanation: Questions 4c and 4d are part of Question 4, inside the 'Powering up' (Level ★★) section.

questions.question: What is the connection between Question 4c/d and the Boris Eldagsen story on a later page?
options: Both are about openly telling others when AI has been used
Both are about food delivery apps
questions.explanation: Both are about openly telling others (a teacher/parent, or the public) when AI has been used to help create something.

questions.question: Select all reasons someone might have ticked 'I didn't think about it' for Question 4c.
options: They didn't consider disclosure as something they needed to do
They actively decided to hide their AI use
They deliberately lied to their teacher
They were told by the teacher not to use AI
questions.explanation: 'I didn't think about it' describes a lack of consideration, not an active decision to hide or lie — those describe different situations.

questions.question: True or False: Question 4c only offers a single Yes/No choice, with no middle option.
questions.explanation: It offers three choices — Yes, No, and I didn't think about it.

questions.question: Which value, repeated across Question 3, Question 4, and the Boris Eldagsen story, connects all three parts of the worksheet?
options: Being honest about how AI helped with your work
questions.explanation: All three sections centre on being honest about how AI helped with something.

questions.question: Boris Eldagsen chose to reveal his AI use even though he could have stayed silent and kept the prize. Which worksheet question explores a similar choice for students?
questions.explanation: Question 4c (telling a teacher or parent about AI use) parallels Eldagsen's choice to disclose rather than stay silent.

questions.question: True or False: The worksheet only raises the idea of disclosure (telling the truth about AI use) in one single question.
questions.explanation: Disclosure/honesty comes up in Question 3 (the essay statements), Question 4c (telling a teacher/parent), and again in the Boris Eldagsen story.

questions.question: Which two feelings does Question 4d offer for reflecting on your disclosure choice?
questions.explanation: The worksheet states: 'How do you feel about that choice now? Confident/ Nervous.'

questions.question: Select all worksheet parts where the idea of 'telling the truth about AI use' appears.
questions.explanation: Question 1's apps table is about data collection, not disclosure of AI use in a student's own work, so it is not part of this pattern.

questions.question: What is Question 4d mainly checking?
options: How the student feels, in hindsight, about their past disclosure choice
How fast the student can type
How many apps the student has downloaded
questions.explanation: Question 4d checks how the student feels, in hindsight, about the disclosure choice they made in 4c.

questions.question: True or False: Feeling 'Nervous' about a past disclosure choice, as asked in Question 4d, might be a sign that a student is unsure whether it was the most honest choice.
questions.explanation: This is a reasonable reflective interpretation the worksheet invites, tying feelings about a choice back to the chapter's honesty theme.

questions.question: Question 5 asks you to explain the 'privacy puzzle problem' to whom?
questions.explanation: Question 5 says: 'Imagine your younger sibling asks you...'

questions.question: According to Question 5, how long should the voice note explanation be?
questions.explanation: Question 5 asks for a voice note of '60-90 seconds'.

questions.question: Select all the voice-recording tools/apps mentioned in Question 5.
questions.explanation: Question 5 names Voice Memo (iPhone), Recorder (Android), and 'any voice tool you have'.

questions.question: In Question 5, the imagined question your younger sibling asks starts: 'What's the privacy puzzle problem? Why can't I just...'
questions.explanation: The full quoted question is: '...Why can't I just tell the app my name?'

questions.question: Question 5 asks you to use 'your own words' and 'your own ___' when explaining the idea.
questions.explanation: The instruction says: 'in your own words, using your own examples.'

questions.question: True or False: Question 5 asks you to write a long essay about the privacy puzzle problem.
questions.explanation: It asks for a spoken voice note of 60-90 seconds, not a written essay.

questions.question: Which section (Level) of the worksheet contains the privacy puzzle problem task?
options: Thinking deeper (at your own pace), Level ★★★
questions.explanation: Question 5 is inside the 'Thinking deeper (at your own pace)' section, Level ★★★.

questions.question: Why might Question 5 ask you to imagine explaining the idea to a YOUNGER sibling, rather than to an adult?
options: Explaining something in simple terms often means you must really understand it yourself
Younger siblings always know more about AI
It is impossible to explain anything to an adult
questions.explanation: Explaining something in simple terms, as if to a younger person, often means you must really understand it yourself first.

questions.question: Based on everything the worksheet covers before Question 5 (apps collecting data, the food delivery example, comfortable vs. safe sharing), the 'privacy puzzle' most likely refers to...
